channel.title: Daily Digest
channel.description: Curated tech blog summaries, inspired by Andrej Karpathy's reading list

item.title: Reading List 05/30/26
item.description: This digest highlights a diverse range of current events including industrial accidents, innovations in nuclear energy, and creative data collection strategies for robotics. It provides a curated overview of significant developments across the construction and technology sectors.

item.title: This Week in Package Management: 30 May 2026
item.description: This post provides a weekly digest of significant security updates and feature releases across major package managers including npm, pnpm, NuGet, Cargo, and Composer. Key highlights include critical security patches for vulnerability exploits and the introduction of new script execution policies to enhance supply chain integrity.

item.title: Notes from May 2026
item.description: This blog post provides a monthly update on the author's personal projects, including new web tools, command-line utilities, and progress on the Helmet open-source project. It also features a curated selection of external readings covering topics such as tech ethics, labor unions in the tech industry, and the socio-technical implications of AI.

item.title: Spot checking polynomial identities
item.description: The article explains the Schwartz-Zippel lemma, demonstrating that checking polynomial identities at a few random points provides high confidence in their validity. It explores how this probabilistic approach serves as an efficient alternative to symbolic verification.

item.title: Microcode inside the Intel 8087 floating-point chip: register exchange
item.description: This article explores the internal microcode of the 1980 Intel 8087 floating-point co-processor. The author reverse-engineers the FXCH instruction to demonstrate how low-level microcode manages register exchanges within the chip's complex architecture.

item.title: Sharing the result of a single Windows Runtime IAsyncOperation among multiple coroutines, part 3
item.description: This article explores technical strategies for managing Windows Runtime IAsyncOperation results across multiple concurrent tasks. It specifically focuses on an implementation pattern that ensures an asynchronous operation is only executed once.

item.title: Arp 114:
item.description: This post features an astrophotography capture of the interacting galaxy pair Arp 114 (NGC 2276 and NGC 2300). It details the technical equipment and processing workflow used to image these galaxies while discussing their unique structural characteristics and tidal interactions.

item.title: Pluralistic: Carneyism without Carney (30 May 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: Cory Doctorow critiques the 'Third Way' political strategy, arguing that politicians who campaign on populist values but govern for elites inevitably breed cynicism and fuel authoritarianism. Using Canada's Liberal Party as a case study, he illustrates how this dissonance facilitates the rise of far-right movements.

item.title: How we contain Claude across products
item.description: This post reviews Anthropic's technical documentation on how they implement sandboxing to secure AI agents like Claude across different environments. It highlights specific isolation technologies used, such as gVisor, Seatbelt, and full VM virtualization to prevent unauthorized data exfiltration.

item.title: Running Python ASGI apps in the browser via Pyodide + a service worker
item.description: Simon Willison shares a new research experiment on running Python ASGI applications directly in the browser using Pyodide and Service Workers. This approach improves upon previous Web Worker methods by properly supporting JavaScript execution within the app, enhancing compatibility for complex tools like Datasette.

item.title: I Am Retiring from Tech to Live Offline
item.description: Chad Whitacre has announced his retirement from the tech industry and open-source development due to the increasing influence of AI. He describes his transition as becoming 'Neo-Amish,' aiming to return to a 1980s-era lifestyle to avoid the psychological impact of modern digital environments.

item.title: Quoting Daniel Jalkut
item.description: This post highlights a perspective from Daniel Jalkut regarding the polarized debate surrounding artificial intelligence. He argues that both extreme opposition and extreme advocacy for AI are misguided.

item.title: Nitpicking the shell history scene in ‘Tron: Legacy’
item.description: The author provides a meticulous analysis of a computer shell history scene from the movie 'Tron: Legacy'. This exploration serves as both a fun retrospective and an educational exercise in evaluating technical accuracy in film.

item.title: What's going on with Gemini?
item.description: This article evaluates Google's Gemini 3.5 Flash, highlighting the performance gap in coding tasks despite its speed and cost. It explores how the model serves Google's internal infrastructure and the strategic challenges the company faces in developing competitive coding agents.

item.title: Composer’s dependency policies
item.description: Composer 2.10 introduces a new configuration policy block that centralizes security advisories, malware reports, and package blocklists. This feature allows developers to subscribe to filter lists, similar to ad blockers, providing proactive protection by blocking flagged packages during both installation and auditing.

item.title: Online (one-pass) algorithms
item.description: This article discusses online (one-pass) algorithms, which allow for the calculation of statistics like sample variance without needing to store the entire dataset. It highlights how these methods process data sequentially, avoiding the multi-pass requirement traditionally associated with such computations.

item.title: Sharing the result of a single Windows Runtime IAsyncOperation among multiple coroutines, part 2
item.description: This post discusses methods for sharing the result of a single Windows Runtime IAsyncOperation across multiple coroutines. It suggests a turn-based approach to handling asynchronous operations in a concurrent environment.

item.title: The UK Government's Low Value Purchase System is a Waste of Time
item.description: The article critiques the UK Government's RM6237 Low Value Purchase System, arguing that it fails to simplify procurement for small businesses. It highlights the bureaucratic hurdles and inefficiencies inherent in the current government contracting process.

item.title: datasette 1.0a31
item.description: Datasette 1.0a31 introduces new write query execution and saved query capabilities, allowing authorized users to modify database content. The release includes an interactive interface for managing SQL updates and inserts with specific permission controls.

item.title: Anthropic's run-rate revenue hits $47 billion
item.description: Anthropic has announced that its annualized run-rate revenue reached $47 billion, continuing a period of explosive growth throughout 2026. This post tracks the company's rapid financial trajectory from $9 billion at the end of 2025 to its current record high.

item.title: Claude Opus 4.8: "a modest but tangible improvement"
item.description: Anthropic has released Claude Opus 4.8, which the company describes as a modest but tangible improvement over previous versions. The update focuses on increased honesty and reducing hallucinations by having the model more frequently acknowledge uncertainty rather than providing unsupported answers.

item.title: llm-anthropic 0.25.1
item.description: The llm-anthropic 0.25.1 release introduces support for the new Claude Opus 4.8 model and adds a fast mode option for eligible accounts. Additionally, it updates the default max_tokens settings for all models to align with their actual maximum output limits.

item.title: markdown-svg-renderer
item.description: Simon Willison introduces a web-based Markdown renderer that specifically handles fenced SVG code blocks. The tool allows users to toggle between rendered SVG images and their source code, supporting direct text input or remote Markdown files.

item.title: It's hard to justify buying a Framework 12
item.description: The author evaluates the value proposition of the Framework 12 laptop by comparing it against Apple's MacBook Neo. Through the lens of purchasing a machine for a high school graduate, the piece highlights how Apple's current offerings have shifted the market standard for price-to-performance.

item.title: Every Enemy Wears Your Face
item.description: This piece explores the psychological phenomenon of projection, where individuals externalize their own traits or insecurities onto others. It examines how the enemies we perceive in our lives often serve as mirrors for our own hidden shadows.

item.title: Notes on Fourier series
item.description: This article provides a mathematical breakdown of Fourier series, explaining how periodic functions can be decomposed into an infinite sum of sinusoids. It details the derivation of coefficients using integration steps and discusses the connection between these series and linear algebra in Hilbert space.

item.title: Knowing about things is cheaper than knowing things
item.description: The author argues that instead of mastering a single complex field, programmers benefit more from obtaining broad, foundational knowledge across many disciplines. This allows developers to identify which specific areas are worth pursuing in-depth based on their unique professional domains.

item.title: Where Are the Economies of Scale in Homebuilding?
item.description: This article investigates the lack of economies of scale in the residential construction industry. It explores the underlying factors contributing to the sector's persistent productivity stagnation.

item.title: Protestware for coding agents
item.description: The author discusses a recent incident where a Java library, jqwik, introduced a hidden command in its code designed to trick AI coding agents by issuing a 'delete' instruction. This act of 'protestware' highlights a growing trend of developers inserting anti-AI resistance into their packages, marking a shift from human-readable banners to machine-readable prompt injection.

item.title: Package managers that package package managers
item.description: This article explores the interconnected nature of software package managers by mapping how different tools can install one another. The author uses data from ecosyste.ms and Repology to visualize which package managers are available within other systems, revealing trends in cross-language tooling and distribution.

item.title: The Costco theory of the internet
item.description: The article introduces 'The Costco Theory of the Internet,' inspired by Sol Price's FedMart philosophy of offering limited choices to increase operational efficiency. It suggests that success in digital spaces often stems from curation and the deliberate choice to ignore certain segments to optimize the core user experience.

item.title: Turning K-L divergence into a metric
item.description: This article discusses the mathematical properties of Kullback-Leibler (K-L) divergence and why it fails to function as a formal metric. It introduces Jeffreys divergence as a potential adjustment to resolve the issue of symmetry.

item.title: Dancing mad with sandboxing
item.description: This post introduces Kefka, a Go-native shell sandbox capable of running coreutils and Python via WebAssembly. It explores the technical challenges and innovative engineering choices behind building this sandboxing environment.

item.title: Gadget Review: Chuwi Minibook X N150 + Linux ★★★★☆
item.description: The author reviews the Chuwi Minibook X N150, a compact and affordable laptop suitable for travel. It highlights the device's portability, affordability, and USB-C compatibility, while noting it performs adequately for basic tasks.

item.title: Notes on optimizing battery life:
item.description: This post explores practical strategies for optimizing battery life in electronic devices by understanding power draw and battery characteristics. It emphasizes the importance of reading datasheets, monitoring discharge curves, and accounting for internal resistance and temperature effects on battery performance.

item.title: Pluralistic: Hold on for dear life (28 May 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: This post explores the intersection of cryptography and technopolitics, specifically focusing on the power of robust encryption to protect privacy against authoritarian surveillance. It highlights how properly implemented cryptographic keys provide near-impenetrable security, enabling individuals to safeguard digital assets and communications from external interference.

item.title: sqlite AGENTS.md
item.description: SQLite has introduced an AGENTS.md file to clarify its policy against accepting AI-generated agentic code contributions, while still welcoming human-verified bug reports. The project has also moved AI-generated reports to a separate forum to manage the influx of submissions.

item.title: Tuning in FM Radio on a 3D Printer Heatbed
item.description: Jeff Geerling investigates whether a 3D printer's heated bed can function as an FM radio antenna. The experiment explores the physical similarities between PCB heatbed traces and antenna designs, testing if they can receive broadcast signals.

How my minimal, memory-safe Go rsync steers clear of vulnerabilities
item.description: This article examines whether implementing a minimal rsync version in the memory-safe Go language effectively prevents common security vulnerabilities. The author analyzes 12 rsync vulnerabilities from 2025 and 2026 to evaluate the security advantages of using Go and a reduced codebase compared to traditional C implementations.

item.title: Weekly Update 505
item.description: Troy Hunt reports on the recent cybercriminal activities of ShinyHunters, specifically regarding their silence following a large ransom payment. The post provides an update on the timeframe and developments surrounding the Instructure data breach incident.

item.title: The Eternal Sloptember
item.description: The author argues that AI agents are fundamentally incapable of replacing human software engineers, describing them as sophisticated statistical models that mimic code rather than understanding it. Despite their usefulness for prototyping and information retrieval, the author contends that their output lacks the necessary polish and reliability for real-world production environments.

item.title: Childhood Computing
item.description: The author reflects on their childhood introduction to computing in a 1992 school computer lab. By sharing personal anecdotes about using limited, disk-based IBM PCs and learning the Logo programming language, the piece highlights how resource constraints fostered deep engagement with technology.

item.title: Signing is for the bad days
item.description: The article explains why digital signatures and supply chain security tools like Sigstore and in-toto are essential, even when they provide no visible benefit during normal operations. It highlights how these tools protect against build server compromises and malicious software substitution, while profiling the contributions of Santiago Torres-Arias to these security frameworks.

item.title: Walking the dog with Claude
item.description: Matt Godbolt discusses the challenge of balancing technical accuracy with engaging presentation in content creation. By using an LLM to interview him, he explores the gap between subject matter experts and effective communicators, citing examples of creators who successfully bridge this divide.

item.title: Building Pi With Pi
item.description: The author reflects on using the AI tool 'Pi' to develop Pi itself, noting how it has shifted the nature of issue tracking. He warns that AI-generated issues often contain confident but inaccurate diagnostic information, creating extra work for maintainers when users submit content not written in their own voice.

item.title: Quoting Armin Ronacher
item.description: Armin Ronacher criticizes the influx of low-quality GitHub issues generated by LLMs, which often contain inaccurate conclusions and unnecessary fluff. He advocates for a return to concise, human-centric reporting that focuses strictly on observed commands, expectations, actual results, and raw logs.

item.title: Mad House — Usborne Creepy Computer Games
item.description: Simon Willison shares a retro project where he used AI to recreate 'Mad House,' a 1983 game from Usborne's classic computer books. By feeding the original book's PDF into Claude, he generated a playable, mobile-friendly JavaScript version of the text-based game.

item.title: Some notes on how we ended up with Palantir & how to replace it
item.description: The article discusses the concerns surrounding government reliance on Palantir and the challenges involved in developing replacements. It emphasizes that replacing such software requires more than just technical alternatives, as the issue is deeply tied to how data is handled and integrated.

item.title: There is only one bad AI scenario
item.description: The author argues that extreme, science-fiction AI doomsday scenarios are unlikely, suggesting instead that the true danger lies in the gradual, administrative mediation of human reality. Through the lens of 'safetyism,' AI may evolve to domesticate humanity by removing all risk and friction, ultimately stifling our evolutionary nature and freedom.

item.title: Don't Roll Your Own ...
item.description: The author argues that developers should stop reinventing standard web functionality, drawing a parallel to the cryptographic maxim 'don't roll your own crypto.' By favoring established browser standards over custom implementations, developers can avoid common pitfalls and improve user experience.

item.title: Reading List 05/23/26
item.description: This reading list covers a diverse range of topics, including industrial waste management, semiconductor supply chain adjustments, and regional resource challenges. It highlights significant real-world issues like water scarcity and innovative solutions for industrial material repurposing.

item.title: This Week in Package Management: 23 May 2026
item.description: This weekly digest covers key updates in package management, including major changes to npm-shrinkwrap.json and security patches in uv and Ruby. It also highlights recent supply chain security incidents involving poisoned VS Code extensions and new feature rollouts in Deno 2.8.

item.title: Hilbert transform as an infinite matrix
item.description: This article explores the Hilbert transform by representing it as an infinite matrix, building upon the relationship between Fourier series coefficients and the transform. It provides a mathematical perspective on how linear operators can be structured using infinite-dimensional matrices.

item.title: Real and imaginary parts
item.description: This post discusses the mathematical process of decomposing complex variable functions into their real and imaginary components. It highlights the author's notes based on Henry Baker's work, which explores expressing f(x + iy) as u(x, y) + i v(x, y).

item.title: Building complex functions out of real parts
item.description: This article explores how to compute elementary complex functions using only real variables and real-valued functions. The author demonstrates that complex operations can be deconstructed into real-variable equivalents, extending the logic used for sine and cosine functions.

item.title: Reverse engineering circuitry in a Spacelab computer from 1980
item.description: This article explores the hardware architecture of the Mitra 125 MS, a French minicomputer used to control the Space Shuttle's Spacelab module. The author reverse-engineers the computer's Arithmetic/Logic Unit (ALU) boards, detailing how the 16-bit processor was constructed from multiple boards rather than a single microprocessor.
